To behave like an ISBN-10, the identifier needs nine data digits followed by a check digit. Pad the Tropicos ID 261 on the left with zeros to make nine digits: 0 0 0 0 0 0 2 6 1.

Weighted sum (weights 10→2):
0×10 + 0×9 + 0×8 + 0×7 + 0×6 + 0×5 + 2×4 + 6×3 + 1×2 = 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 8 + 18 + 2 = 28.

Let d be the check digit.  (28 + d) mod 11 = 0 ⇒ d = 5.

Therefore the ISBN-10 check digit corresponding to the Tropicos ID 261 is 5.
Treat the nine-digit body of the ISBN as the Tropicos ID padded with leading zeros: 000000261.
Weights 10→2:
0×10 + 0×9 + 0×8 + 0×7 + 0×6 + 0×5 + 2×4 + 6×3 + 1×2 = 28.
Let d be the check digit with weight 1.
(28 + d) mod 11 = 0 ⇒ d = 5.
So the ISBN-10 check digit would be 5.

Identify chemicals commonly used in ELISA in the paper: alkaline phosphatase and horseradish peroxidase. Their EC numbers: 3.1.3.1 and 1.11.1.7. Alphabetize chemicals (Alkaline phosphatase before Horseradish peroxidase). Produce semicolon-separated EC numbers.
The virus detection methods in the 2016 SPFMV and SPCSV study relied on ELISA assays, whose most common enzyme conjugates are alkaline phosphatase and horseradish peroxidase. Their EC numbers are 3.1.3.1 and 1.11.1.7 respectively. Alphabetizing the chemicals (alkaline phosphatase before horseradish peroxidase) yields the order 3.1.3.1;1.11.1.7.
